title: Baltimore harbor gains ‘floating wetlands’ and a hint of its marshy past
summary: The National Aquarium’s newest exhibit is a  10,000-square-foot “floating wetlands,” an artificial saltmarsh habitat planted in buoyant plastic-fiber mats in the Inner Harbor next to the aquarium.
content:
By Jeremy Cox

Chesapeake Bay Journal

The National Aquarium’s newest exhibit is putting the “wet” in wetlands.

The Baltimore attraction opened a new exhibit Aug. 9 in the Inner Harbor: a 10,000-square-foot “floating wetlands,” an artificial saltmarsh habitat planted in buoyant plastic-fiber mats.

The $14 million project was underwritten in large part by CFG Bank. It accomplishes several objectives, said Jack Cover, the aquarium’s longtime general curator.

By taking up nutrients, the plants help improve water quality in the ecologically troubled harbor. The greenery reintroduces a type of habitat that the harbor long ago lost to development. And the aquarium gains a new educational display, complete with a floating dock and signage.

“What we’re trying to do is bring the Chesapeake Bay to the city,” Cover said.

The exhibit is situated in a finger of water between the aquarium’s two main buildings. It bobs atop 25 feet of water where barges once docked to offload coal at the Pratt Street Power Plant (now home to a Phillips Seafood restaurant, a Hard Rock Café and the Baltimore Banner).

Work began on the installation last fall. It was assembled in pieces and connected at the site. Instead of soil, the plants are moored in pre-drilled holes in black, foam-like material.

That material, in turn, rests atop a submerged metal grate whose height in the water column can be controlled by a pontoon ballast system. As the plants get bigger, adding more weight to the grate, aquarium staff can add air into the pontoons to increase buoyancy and prevent the exhibit from sinking, Cover said.

Baltimore is the latest in a growing number of places — a list that includes Boston and Chicago — betting on floating wetlands to restore at least some of the “ecosystem services” they lost to an earlier generation of development.

By replacing marshy shorelines with hard surfaces hundreds of years ago, cities stripped away an important filter for stormwater pollution, experts say. Nearby waterways like the Inner Harbor quickly became choked with nutrients, sediment and other contaminants, triggering harmful algal blooms that left their waters all but ecologically dead.

The long-gone marshes also served as a refuge for fish and birds. Architects of the new floating wetlands hope that by reconstructing what had been destroyed, they can attract life back to the watery fringes of urban centers.

“You never know what’s going to come here,” Cover said, adding that human observers and wildlife cameras at the new wetland have already begun spotting creatures rarely seen in the city, including night herons, mallards and even two river otters. “If you build it, they will come.”

The ballast system is just one of the design features believed to be unique to these floating wetlands.

Tubes blow a steady stream of air into the water around the plants. It’s the same technology used in the aquarium’s tanks to add oxygen to water and keep them from becoming stagnant, Cover said. If that were to happen, algal and bacterial blooms wouldn’t be far behind.

The floating wetlands are also thought to be the first of their kind to incorporate a central channel within their footprint. The meandering waterway, which is best viewed from a higher vantage point, such as the adjacent arched walkway, mimics shallow water habitat for wildlife.

The aquarium brought in 100 bags of oyster shells — each dotted with lab-grown spat, or baby oysters — and spread them across the grate. Cover and his colleagues hope that, as the young bivalves grow, the notorious bottom feeders will filter increasing amounts of pollution from the harbor.

The wetland was a product of 14 years of trial and error. Aquarium staff began experimenting with floating wetland technology in 2010 with the construction of a modest 200-square-foot installation. It marked the first time in the U.S. that the technology had been deployed in a brackish tidal system, where it would have to overcome the harsh exposure to salt and the ebbs and flows of tides.

Lessons came fast. Canada geese dined on the grasses with gusto, leaving little behind. (Later versions would include low fencing around the plants.) And the original anchor system failed.

A total of four prototypes preceded the final version. The fourth, established in 2017, is the only one that remains floating. It is still festooned with healthy grasses and plants, tied up near the northwest corner of the same inlet where the new wetland was built.

Staff members and volunteers began planting nearly 40,000 grass and shrub specimens in the latest version of the wetlands in May. By July, a dense, green tableau was already on display, mostly represented by wavy strands of native cordgrass. Cover suspects that the glut of nutrients in Baltimore’s rainwater is helping to stoke the immense growth.

“It really is a dream come true,” Cover said, surveying the burgeoning flora on a recent morning.

He acknowledges that it’s hard to say how much the wetland will help clean up the harbor. The water body is an offshoot of the Patapsco River, a Chesapeake Bay tributary. It would almost certainly be too pricey to replicate the project at a scale large enough to replace wetlands lost to development, land subsidence and sea level rise across the Bay region.

But, Cover added, it does demonstrate that nature, if given a helping hand, can be brought back to life.

“There’s a common misconception that if I want to see nature, I have to get in a car and drive to a state park,” he said. “Nature is here. We just have to bring back some of these micro-habitats that animals seek.”

The floating wetland will be open during the aquarium’s normal business hours as long as the weather cooperates. No aquarium admission fee is necessary.
